keyVerseText: And Azel had six sons, whose names are these, Azrikam, Bocheru, and Ishmael, and Sheariah, and Obadiah, and Hanan. All these were the sons of Azel.
rootMeaning: The name שְׁעַרְיָה (Sheariah) derives from the Hebrew root שָׁעַר (shâʻar), which involves the concept of acting as a gatekeeper or calculating, combined with the divine element יָהּ (Jah), a shortened form of Jehovah. Literally, this can be understood as "Jah has stormed" or "valued by Jehovah," implying divine protection or valuation at a gate or threshold. This root sense highlights not only a literal guardian role but also a figurative sense of being esteemed or reckoned by God, adding depth beyond the simple English transliteration.
usageInScripture: The name Sheariah appears twice in Scripture, consistently translated as "and Sheariah," indicating it is used as a proper name without variation in meaning. Both occurrences refer to an individual, specifically a Benjamite descendant of Saul, emphasizing a personal identity rather than a conceptual term. This consistency shows the name's function as a marker of lineage and heritage within the biblical narrative.
theologicalSignificance: The meaning of Sheariah as "valued by Jehovah" or "Jah has stormed" underscores the intimate relationship between God's sovereignty and His people. It reflects the truth that believers are not only protected by God but also esteemed and reckoned as precious in His sight. In the Christian faith, this name reminds us of our identity in Christ, who secures and values His followers at the gates of life and eternity. Recognizing this divine valuation encourages trust in God's providence and affirms the believer’s place within His covenant community.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Chronicles 8:38, Sheariah is listed among the six sons of Azel, grounding the name in a concrete family lineage within the tribe of Benjamin. The inclusion of Sheariah here highlights the importance of heritage and God's ongoing work through His people. The name's meaning enriches the passage by suggesting that this individual is not only part of a genealogical record but also carries the weight of being "valued by Jehovah," which points to God's faithful preservation of His covenant line.
